analysis.one_liner: Caps US prescription drug prices at the lowest price charged in eleven other wealthy countries.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Health committee: it was referred there on the day it was introduced and died there when the 118th Congress ended, with two sponsors and no floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Health and Human Services Secretary to set a yearly maximum price for every prescription drug, based on the lowest price the drug sells for in countries like Japan, Germany, the UK, France, Canada, and Australia. Those capped prices would apply to Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA care, federal employee insurance, and Indian Health Service programs, and drug makers would also have to offer the same price to uninsured people and people with private insurance. Companies that charged more would face a civil penalty worth five times the excess revenue, with the money going to the National Institutes of Health for drug research.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors and disabled people on Medicare, low-income people on Medicaid, children on CHIP, military families and veterans on TRICARE and VA care, federal employees, people served by the Indian Health Service, and uninsured or privately insured Americans who today often pay the highest drug prices in the developed world.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare, Medicaid, VA patients and the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: Caps the retail list price of every prescription drug at the lowest price it sells for among eleven reference countries (Japan, Germany, the UK, France, Italy, Canada, Australia, Spain, the Netherlands, Switzerland, and Sweden), for drugs sold through Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA, FEHBP, and Indian Health programs.

Requires manufacturers to offer drugs at that same reference price to people with no insurance and to people with private coverage, so the countries' lowest price follows the drug everywhere rather than only inside federal programs.

Imposes a civil penalty on noncompliant manufacturers equal to five times the amount they overcharged federal programs that year, with the collected penalties transferred to NIH to fund drug research and development.
For drugs not available in at least three reference countries, lets HHS set the price based on the drug's therapeutic value, patient access, and research and development costs.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose US prices — typically the highest in the world — would be cut to international reference levels, plus pharmacy benefit managers and intermediaries whose spread on high-priced drugs would shrink. Taxpayers and beneficiaries would pay less.

drawbacks.text: Capping prices at foreign reference levels could reduce the revenue that funds research into new drugs, an honest supporter must weigh this against the fact that penalties collected under the bill are directed to NIH for drug research.

Setting a price for every prescription drug each year is a large administrative undertaking for HHS, and for drugs sold in fewer than three reference countries the price would rest on the Secretary's judgment calls rather than a market benchmark.
The cap applies to list prices across private insurance as well as federal programs, a broader intervention into private markets than narrower Medicare-only price negotiation approaches.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the benefit is direct and large: Americans pay several times what people in peer countries pay for the same drugs, and this bill targets exactly that gap, including for the uninsured. The main cost falls on pharmaceutical company revenues, with a real but debated risk of somewhat less investment in new drugs — partly offset by the bill's own penalty-funded NIH research stream. The design is aggressive but coherent; the bill's failure had nothing to do with its merits being tested, because it never received a hearing, markup, or vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health committee on the same day in June 2023, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced S. 2044 on June 20, 2023, joined by one cosponsor, Sen. Peter Welch.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in either chamber, and it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off, since the US prices that are highest among peer countries remain in place for Medicare, Medicaid, and private payers. The two senators who sponsored it saw their proposal die without ever being debated.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap drug prices at international reference levels.

for.name: Sen. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the only cosponsor it attracted.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral: no hearing, no markup, no vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a vote, so no party split is on the record; its two sponsors were both Democrats, and no senator spoke against it on the floor.

industries.note: US drug prices are typically the highest in the developed world, and this bill would cap them at the lowest price charged in eleven peer countries, hitting the manufacturers' largest and most profitable market. That is precisely the price gap American patients and federal programs pay.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug pricing intermediaries
industries.note: These middlemen profit from spreads and rebates tied to high list prices; a hard price ceiling that also applies to cash-paying uninsured customers would compress the margins they live on.
The reference price cap applies to generic drugs too, but generic prices are usually far below brand-name reference levels, so the practical impact on this segment is small.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: The bill requires manufacturer prices plus cost-sharing under private plans to come in at or below the reference price, lowering drug costs for private plans and their enrollees.
